extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners and other attorneys appearing before the USPTO; Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) staff; administrative law judges; parties in USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural rules the USPTO (and its ALJ) applies in attorney disciplinary proceedings, including grounds for discipline, procedural consequences for failing to answer, factors for selecting sanctions, and rules on interim suspension and exclusion from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to timely file an answer
rubrics_metrics.description: "Failure to timely file an answer will constitute an admission of the allegations in the complaint and may result in entry of default judgment." (37 C.F.R. § 11.36(e))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a respondent does not file an answer, the allegations in the complaint are deemed admitted and may be entered as findings of fact; courts have granted motions for default judgment in such circumstances (e.g., In re Riley, D2013-04). The decision-maker may treat admitted allegations as the basis for findings and sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal acts reflecting adversely on honesty/trustworthiness/fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct involving a criminal act or acts that reflect adversely on the practitioner's honesty, trustworthiness, or fitness as a practitioner is proscribed. (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convictions for illegal possession of controlled substances and carrying a concealed weapon were treated as reflecting adversely on honesty, trustworthiness, and fitness, violating § 11.804(b). Case law supports suspension/exclusion based on felony convictions even before appellate completion (e.g., U.S. v. Friedland; In re Jones).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice is proscribed. (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to respond to correspondence from OED and to court Orders undermines public confidence in the profession's ability to regulate itself and is prejudicial to the administration of justice; an attorney who does not defend himself in disciplinary proceedings cannot be expected to properly represent others before the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interim suspension upon serious crime conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Director may impose an interim suspension when OED requests suspension based on allegations that a registrant was convicted of a serious crime. (37 C.F.R. § 11.25; 35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. § 11.59)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may request interim suspension based on convictions (examples: possession of controlled substances, possession of methamphetamine). Notices and requests for interim suspension are sent under § 11.25 procedures; a Final Order may suspend the practitioner on an interim basis pending further proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to suspend or exclude practitioners
rubrics_metrics.description: The PTO has authority to suspend or exclude a practitioner from practice before the PTO under 35 U.S.C. § 32 and 37 C.F.R. § 11.19.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a registered PTO attorney fails to comply with professional obligations, PTO authority supports suspension or exclusion; courts have upheld summary suspensions based on felony convictions (citing Chaganti v. Lee and other authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors to consider before imposing disciplinary sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sanctioning a practitioner, the Court must consider the following four factors: (1) Whether the practitioner has violated a duty owed to client, to the public, to the legal system, or to the profession; (2) Whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) The amount of the actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct; and (4) The existence of any aggravating or mitigating factors. (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four enumerated factors are applied to determine appropriate sanctions; the record is evaluated against each factor (duty breached, mental state, injury, and aggravation/mitigation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating and mitigating factors (including ABA Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court looks to the American Bar Association Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions when assessing sanctions and evaluates aggravating and mitigating factors; the respondent bears the burden to raise mitigating circumstances. (See ABA Standards; 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.36(c) and 11.49 cited)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors in this case included failure to accept responsibility, a pattern of similar convictions, and repeated failures to respond to OED and court orders. Mitigating factors must be affirmatively raised by the respondent with nexus to the misconduct; failure to present mitigation supports harsher sanctions, potentially the maximum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern of misconduct as an aggravating factor
rubrics_metrics.description: A pattern of misconduct (e.g., repeated similar convictions and repeated failures to respond to disciplinary correspondence) is an aggravating factor supporting increased sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court regarded similar prior convictions and repeated non-responsiveness as evidence of a pattern of misconduct, which contributes to justification for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service and notice requirements and consequences of noncompliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Disciplinary notices, Orders, and complaints must be served (e.g., via certified mail to addresses provided under 37 C.F.R. § 11.11); an Answer to the Complaint is required within prescribed time (e.g., within 30 days of Final Order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mailing to addresses where OED reasonably believes the respondent receives mail (with return receipts) constitutes proper service; failure to respond after proper service can lead to default and entry of judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion from practice as appropriate sanction when factors support it
rubrics_metrics.description: When violations of USPTO Rules, aggravating factors, intentional conduct, potential/actual injury, and absence of mitigating factors are present, exclusion from practice before the USPTO (in patent, trademark, and other non-patent matters) is an appropriate sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on the four sanctioning factors and the presence of multiple aggravating factors and no mitigation, the Court concluded exclusion (maximum sanction) was warranted in this case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on respondent to raise defenses/mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden is on Respondent to raise any affirmative defenses or mitigating circumstances and specify their nexus to the misconduct. (Cited: 13 C.F.R. §§ 11.36(c) and 11.49 in the decision)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to appear or to file an amended response/answer forfeits the opportunity to present mitigation or defenses; absent such evidence, the court may treat the record as showing aggravating factors and impose maximum sanctions.
